title: Postscript and Zweig commentary

claims.text: A single exceptional holding can dominate a long investment record. Preserve this concentration and outcome dependence when assessing the evidence for a broader method.
Distinguishing skill from luck in an exceptional result is difficult; preparation can improve opportunity handling without promising a repeatable windfall.

Reject treating an estimated liquidation value equal to purchase cost as proof that a concentrated holding carried very little financial risk. Realization, liabilities and adverse change remain uncertain.

assimilation: Retain the GEICO example as a disclosed exception to mechanical selling and broad diversification, not a newly validated concentration rule. Attribute outcomes to their actual sources and keep appraisal uncertainty visible even when an investment later succeeds.
adversarial_review: The main text says roughly one-fifth of fund assets while commentary says 25%; retain the discrepancy pending source reconciliation. A negotiated half-interest with influence is not equivalent to an ordinary retail position. Exceptional eventual gains cannot certify initial risk, and holding after apparent overvaluation complicates a simple buy-cheap/sell-at-value interpretation. The book itself declines to promise a similar result to every disciplined investor.
memory_delta: Audit performance concentration and distinguish accessible decisions from privileged deals. Do not retrofit a lucky or skillful outlier into a universal rule; retain exceptions and uncertainty alongside the core process.
